title: Not the thing, my view
hookLine: if something outside pains you, it's your judgment of it, and that you can change (Meditations 8.47)

lines: THE STORY WE TELL ABOUT IT.
cards: It's raining on the day of the picnic. One person says: great, ruined. Another says: fine, we'll eat in the car, it'll be an adventure.
Same rain. Same car. Or two people get the same curt email from the boss.
One spends the evening furious. The other shrugs: she's probably slammed this week. The email didn't change.
What changed was the story each of them told about it. Marcus kept coming back, in his notebook, to that gap between what happens and what we make of it.

teach.h: IT IS NOT THIS THING THAT DISTURBS THEE.
teach.b: Here's how Book Eight, section forty-seven, begins in George Long's translation: "If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs thee, but thy own judgment about it."
And it's in your power, he adds, to wipe out that judgment now. It's an old Stoic idea.
Marcus had read Epictetus, the former slave turned teacher, who said something very close: people are troubled not by things, but by their opinions about things. It's easy to hear this wrong.
Marcus isn't saying pain is imaginary. A broken arm hurts. Grief is real.
He's pointing at the second layer: the story on top. This shouldn't be happening. This always happens to me.
This is a disaster. That layer is judgment, and judgment is yours to examine. Then Marcus goes further in the same passage.
If what bothers you is something in your own character, who's stopping you from correcting it? If it's that you're not doing something you know is right, why not do it instead of complaining?
And if something too strong for you really stands in the way, don't grieve, because the cause isn't yours. So this isn't just changing your mind. It's a sorting.
Some things you reframe. Some you act on. Some you let go.
What you can almost always do is notice the story and ask whether it's true.
Your line: not the thing, my view.

how: Readers of the Stoics often practice separating events from judgments, sometimes by writing down what happened and then the story they told about it; modern cognitive therapy draws on a similar idea.

o: a former slave who became a Stoic teacher
a Roman emperor who ruled before Marcus
a Greek god of calm and clear judgment

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: not things, but opinions about things
who stops you from correcting it?
don't grieve; the cause isn't yours

s: a broken arm hurts. he's pointing at the judgment we add on top.
Marcus had read Epictetus, who taught that people are troubled by opinions about things.
the passage also says to act when you can
if you're not doing what's right, why not do it instead of complaining?

games.q: something is bothering you, and you realize it's that you haven't done something you know is right. what does Marcus say?
o: change how you feel about it.
games.why: in the same passage, Marcus asks: why not act rather than complain?

practice: Let one small complaint come up, the traffic, a coworker, the weather, and say it inside the way you usually do. Then say it plainly, without the story: what actually happened?
Notice the judgment you added, ask if it's true, and try one new sentence about it.

wordCard.voice: Epictetus, the former slave and teacher Marcus read: people are troubled not by things but by their opinions about them. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a judgment, an assumption, one's take on a thing. Marcus uses it elsewhere in the notebook for the view we add to events.

carryVoice: Your line: the story on top. You can almost always notice it, and ask whether it's true. Day two hundred eight, done.

sources.q: If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs thee, but thy own judgment about it.
